content: Ferrous chloride, also known as iron(II) chloride, is a chemical compound with the formula FeCl₂. It is a paramagnetic solid that has a high melting point and is typically obtained as an off-white solid. When crystallized from water, it forms a greenish tetrahydrate, which is the most commonly encountered form in both commercial and laboratory settings. A dihydrate form of the compound also exists. Ferrous chloride is soluble in water, and its aqueous solutions appear yellow. Production Hydrated forms of ferrous chloride are produced by treating waste materials from steel production with hydrochloric acid. These solutions are often referred to as spent acid, particularly when the hydrochloric acid is not fully consumed. Spent acid requires proper treatment before disposal. Ferrous chloride is also a byproduct of titanium production, as some titanium ores contain iron. Laboratory Preparation Ferrous chloride can be conveniently prepared in the laboratory by adding iron powder to a solution of methanol and concentrated hydrochloric acid under an inert atmosphere. This reaction produces a methanol solvate, which, when heated under vacuum at approximately 160°C, yields anhydrous FeCl₂. Analogous methods can be used to prepare related compounds such as FeBr₂ and FeI₂. Another laboratory synthesis involves the reaction of FeCl₃ with chlorobenzene. FeCl₂ is soluble in tetrahydrofuran (THF), a common solvent for chemical reactions. In one of the classic syntheses of ferrocene, Wilkinson prepared FeCl₂ by heating FeCl₃ with iron powder in THF. At high temperatures, ferric chloride (FeCl₃) decomposes to form ferrous chloride (FeCl₂). Reactions Ferrous chloride forms complexes with a variety of ligands. It reacts with two molar equivalents of chloride ions to produce specific salts. Related compounds, such as various anionic salts, can be synthesized using similar methods. Applications Ferrous chloride has several niche applications, although related compounds like ferrous sulfate and ferric chloride are more widely used. In addition to its role in laboratory synthesis of iron complexes, ferrous chloride serves as a reducing and flocculating agent in wastewater treatment, particularly for wastes containing chromate. It is also a precursor to hydrated iron(III) oxides, which are used as magnetic pigments. Furthermore, ferrous chloride is employed as a reducing agent in numerous organic synthesis reactions.
